data.q: What is the return type of an async method that does not return a value?
o: void
Task
Task<void>
ValueTask
data.e: Async methods that do not return a value should return Task. Returning void prevents the caller from awaiting the method and makes exception handling difficult.

data.q: Which method should be used to avoid capturing the current SynchronizationContext when awaiting a Task?
o: Task.Run()
ConfigureAwait(false)
Task.Yield()
Task.Delay(0)
data.e: ConfigureAwait(false) instructs the awaiter not to capture and marshal back to the original SynchronizationContext, improving performance and avoiding deadlocks in library code.

data.q: What happens to exceptions thrown in an async void method?
o: They are caught by the nearest try/catch block.
They are stored in the returned Task.
They are raised on the SynchronizationContext or ThreadPool, potentially crashing the application.
They are silently ignored.
data.e: Exceptions in async void methods are not captured in a Task. They are posted to the SynchronizationContext (UI thread) or the ThreadPool, often resulting in an unhandled exception that terminates the process.

data.q: What is the primary difference between Task.Run and Task.Factory.StartNew?
o: Task.Run is synchronous; StartNew is asynchronous.
Task.Run defaults to TaskScheduler.Default (ThreadPool); StartNew defaults to TaskScheduler.Current.
Task.Run accepts Action only; StartNew accepts Func<Task>.
There is no difference; they are aliases.
data.e: Task.Run uses TaskScheduler.Default (ThreadPool) by default, making it safer for offloading work. Task.Factory.StartNew captures TaskScheduler.Current, which can lead to unexpected behavior if called on a UI thread.

data.q: How does Parallel.ForEach handle the degree of parallelism by default?
o: It uses exactly one thread.
It uses the maximum number of threads available in the ThreadPool.
It uses a heuristic based on workload and core count, adjustable via MaxDegreeOfParallelism.
It creates a new thread for every item.
data.e: Parallel.ForEach dynamically adjusts the number of threads based on the workload and system resources. MaxDegreeOfParallelism can limit this.

data.q: Which type is the recommended return type for an async method that returns a value in high-performance scenarios to avoid allocations?
o: Task<TResult>
ValueTask<TResult>
Task
TResult
data.e: ValueTask<TResult> is a struct that can avoid heap allocation when the result is available synchronously or when using pooled objects (e.g., IValueTaskSource).

data.q: What is the result of awaiting Task.WhenAll if one of the provided tasks faults?
o: It returns immediately with the first exception.
It waits for all tasks to complete, then throws an AggregateException containing all exceptions.
It throws the first exception immediately and cancels the other tasks.
It completes successfully ignoring the faulted task.
data.e: Task.WhenAll waits for all tasks to finish. If any fault, it throws an AggregateException containing all exceptions from all faulted tasks (though `await` unwraps the first one).

data.q: Which interface must a class implement to support asynchronous disposal (await using)?
o: IDisposable
IAsyncDisposable
IAsyncEnumerable
IValueTaskSource
data.e: IAsyncDisposable provides the DisposeAsync method, allowing resource cleanup that requires asynchronous operations (e.g., flushing buffers).

o: A token that is already cancelled.
A token that can never be cancelled.
A token linked to the parent operation.
A token that throws OperationCanceledException immediately.
data.e: CancellationToken.None is a default empty struct representing a token that will never be cancelled. It is used when cancellation is not supported.

data.q: In PLINQ (Parallel LINQ), what does AsOrdered() do?
o: Sorts the results ascending.
Preserves the ordering of the source sequence in the output, potentially reducing performance.
Orders the execution of threads.
Throws if the source is not ordered.
data.e: AsOrdered forces PLINQ to buffer and reorder results to match the source sequence order, which adds overhead compared to unordered execution.

data.q: What is the behavior of 'await foreach' when iterating an IAsyncEnumerable?
o: It blocks the thread until the entire collection is loaded.
It asynchronously waits for each element to be produced by the enumerator.
It runs the enumeration in parallel on multiple threads.
It converts the stream to a List<T> first.
data.e: await foreach consumes an IAsyncEnumerable by asynchronously awaiting each MoveNextAsync call, allowing backpressure and non-blocking iteration.

data.q: Why is 'async void' generally discouraged except for event handlers?
o: It is slower than async Task.
It prevents the caller from awaiting the operation and complicates error handling.
It does not support cancellation tokens.
It cannot use the await keyword.
data.e: Async void methods cannot be awaited, exceptions escape the method context (crashing apps), and callers cannot track completion. They exist solely for event handler signatures.

data.q: What is the purpose of Task.Yield()?
o: To cancel the current task.
To force the method to run synchronously.
To asynchronously yield control back to the current context/scheduler, allowing other work to run.
To create a completed task.
data.e: Task.Yield() creates an awaitable that yields control to the current SynchronizationContext or TaskScheduler, useful for keeping UI responsive or forcing async execution.

data.q: When using Task.WhenAny, what happens to the other tasks that are not the first to complete?
o: They are automatically cancelled.
They continue running in the background.
They are disposed immediately.
They throw TaskCanceledException.
data.e: Task.WhenAny completes when the first task finishes. The remaining tasks continue executing; it is the developer's responsibility to await or handle them later to avoid unobserved exceptions.

data.q: What is the correct way to report progress from a background task to the UI thread using the standard library?
o: Pass a UI control reference to the task.
Use Task.Run with Dispatcher.Invoke.
Use IProgress<T> / Progress<T> which captures the SynchronizationContext at construction.
Use a static ConcurrentQueue.
data.e: Progress<T> captures the SynchronizationContext (e.g., UI thread) when instantiated. Calling Report() marshals the callback to that context, making it thread-safe for UI updates.

data.q: Which statement about 'async' and 'await' keywords is true?
o: 'async' makes a method run on a background thread automatically.
'await' blocks the calling thread until the task completes.
'async' enables the 'await' keyword and causes the compiler to generate a state machine.
'await' can be used in any method without the 'async' modifier.
data.e: The 'async' modifier tells the compiler to rewrite the method into a state machine. It does not inherently make code run in parallel. 'await' asynchronously yields control, it does not block.
